If hearts are not breaking, South needs some kind of squeeze. East is likely to have length in hearts (due to West's club length) and a double squeeze may be possible with diamonds as the suit guarded by both defenders.

South should begin by drawing another round of trump to which both defenders follow. Another club can now be ruffed in the closed hand. South can cash 3 rounds of hearts, noting East's length in the suit. A diamond is played to the dummy and North's last spade will squeeze both defenders.

East must keep his heart as a guard to South's ♥2. East thus pitches a diamond, transferring the sole defensive guard to the West hand. South pitches the ♥2 and West is now squeezed. A club discard will set up North's last club. West must also pitch a diamond and South will take the last 2 tricks in diamonds.

Double squeezes mature with 1 loser. South starts with 2 losers (1 in diamonds and 1 in hearts), but the dummy reversal technique of ruffing 3 clubs in the South hand increases South's trick count to 12. The double squeeze produces trick 13.

In every double squeeze, both defenders are squeezed in a common suit (diamonds in this hand). That suit must contain an entry. Each defender is also solely responsible for guarding another suit (East guards hearts, West guards clubs).

Several forms of double squeeze exist. Depending on the nature of the winners and entries in the threat suits, a double squeeze may not function or it may be difficult to play in the ending. The above position is fairly straight forward. South must be careful, however, to cash his top hearts before playing North's last trump.

notes: West leads the ♠10 against 6NT. The opening spade lead is won in dummy. West's heart preempt has marked him with all 7 outstanding hearts and East with the ♦A. If West has the ♦Q, South should be able to succeed.

A diamond is played from North. If East wins the ♦A, West eventually will be subjected to a simple squeeze. East must, therefore, duck and South wins the ♦K. The spades and clubs are cashed. On the last club, West must pitch a diamond coming down to a singleton ♦Q. South exits a diamond.
If East plays low, West is left on lead and endplayed. If East overtakes, he establishes a diamond trick in dummy. East, with only diamonds left, must allow South to reach this stranded winner.

This ending is called a winkle. A winkle is a 2-loser squeeze that forces the defense to block a suit. Declarer can take advantage of the blockage by exiting that suit, forcing either the lead into a tenace or the building of a winner in the blocked suit.

East cannot gain by ruffing. He will discard and South wins. South should play a heart and ruff with the ♠A. A trump trick has likely been promoted for East, but he will use it to overruff the dummy when South's last heart is ruffed.

The only danger remaining is that the defense may be able to promote a second trump trick. South must figure out the best way to return to his hand to minimize this danger. If South returns to the ♣A the contract will fail whenever East has 5 clubs. If South returns to his hand with a diamond ruff the contract will fail whenever East has 7 diamonds.

The 7-2 diamond break is less likely than the 5-1 club break especially considering the defenders' silence in the bidding. South should return to his hand with a diamond ruff. South's last heart is ruffed in dummy and overruffed by East. On East's diamond return, South can ruff low, draw trump, and take the balance.

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 3♠. West's club lead is won in dummy. South must avoid the loss of 3 diamond tricks and 2 trump tricks.
If South crosses in hearts and plays a diamond to the ♦K and ♦A, East will return a trump. If East has the ♦Q, South will have to guess the trump position to make the contract.

South can make the contract without guessing by leading the ♦4 from dummy at trick 2. If East has the ♦Q, South will have held his diamond losers to 2. He can afford to lose 2 trump tricks if necessary.

If West has the ♦Q, he cannot afford to play trump from his side of the table without holding South's trump losers to 1. If West has all 4 trumps he can exit with a low trump. South plays a second round of diamonds. If West has the ♦A, he will not be able to prevent a diamond ruff except by surrendering 1 of his trump tricks.

Upon winning the ♦Q, West will exit passively. A diamond is played. For South to have any problem, East must win the ♦A and return a trump. South can either finesse or win the ♠A and be certain of making the contract.

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 5♥. West's club lead goes to the ♣A and East returns the suit, South winning the ♣K. South draws 2 rounds of trump. West discards on the second round.

West has shown at least 5 cards in spades and a 5 card minor (presumably clubs) with his Michael's cue bid. South will not be able to ruff both of his club losers in dummy as East will be able to overruff.
South may be able to put the West hand under pressure. West must be 5125. He must hold the ♦K for the contract to have a chance. The bidding and early defense suggest the ♠A and ♠K are split.

South can draw the last trump and take a diamond finesse. The ♦A is cashed, dropping the ♦K. Another diamond trick is cashed. The ♦5 is ruffed by South. On this trick West is forced to come down to 2 spades and 2 clubs.

South now leads the ♠2. If West wins the trick, he will be endplayed, forced to concede a trick in either spades or clubs. If West plays low, an honour is played from North which East wins. East has only spades left and must play one. South ruffs and West's spade honour will show up. The dummy will be high.

notes: West leads the ♦6 against 6♠. West's diamond lead (an obvious singleton) is won by South. A top spade reveals the 3-0 trump break and marks West with 3712 distribution. It looks like South will need some sort of trump squeeze against East.

South should continue with a low trump to the dummy. The ♥A is cashed for a club discard. A heart is ruffed high. South crosses again in spades, drawing West's last trump in the process. On dummy's last heart East is forced to discard a club while South ruffs.
South now ducks a club. If East wins, South will be able to establish a club trick by ruffing. If East plays low, allowing West to win the club trick, West's only hope is to play a heart.

South can take the ruff in either hand and subsequently squeeze East. If South ruffs in the dummy, for example, he can next cross to his hand in diamonds. On the play of the last trump, East is squeezed in diamonds and clubs.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 7♠. West's opening diamond lead should be won in the South hand. Dummy entries should be conserved as South's plan should be to try to learn West's shape.

If it turns out that West has a singleton heart, South will need that heart to be the ♥6 or ♥8. Several dummy entries will be needed to pick up the hearts. South should play a club to the ♣A and play a second club, ruffing. South crosses in trumps. North's last club is played and ruffed with the ♠A. South crosses again in trumps.

West has followed to 2 rounds of spades and 3 rounds of clubs. The ♦A confirms that West has 7 diamonds. The only hope is that his thirteenth card is the ♥6 or ♥8. The ♥9 is played, covered by East, and won by South. The appearance of the ♥8 from West is good news. North has 2 entries (a diamond ruff and a spade) to take 2 more finesses in hearts.

South now plays a heart. East wins the ♥A and returns a diamond, killing the link with dummy before hearts can be unblocked.

On the second diamond, West's discard marks him with a stopper in hearts or in clubs. Thanks to South's foresight in clubs, the contract still has a chance on a double guard squeeze if West started with 7312 and 2 of the ♣Q, ♣10, and ♣9.

Dummy's diamonds are run. South must unblock his heart honour and keep a spade. On the last diamond East must pitch a heart. South lets go of a club and West must discard his last club. The ♥J will take care of South's last spade. South will have a proven finesse in clubs at trick 12.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 6NT. West's spade lead should be won with the ♠A. West's spade preempt makes East a favourite to hold the ♦Q and length in that suit. If that is the case, South can succeed on a rare 2-loser squeeze, a double stepping stone.
The ♦A and ♦K should be cashed, followed by 7 rounds of clubs. On the last club, a spade from East will allow South to cash the ♥K and play a diamond to East as a stepping stone to the ♥A.

East must therefore discard a heart on the last club, but the same fate awaits West who now holds the only heart guard. He must pitch a spade. The ♥K is cashed and a spade exit makes use of West as a stepping stone to the ♥A.

review.hl: NCA NCK NCQ NCJ NC9 NC8 NC7

notes: West leads the ♠J against 3NT. West's spade lead is won by South. The only possible problem is a 4-0 club break and a 5-2 spade break. South may be able to guard against this distribution by playing for a compound suicide squeeze.

South should start by cashing a high club from the closed hand. The ♣Q will be needed as a later dummy entry. When East turns up with a club stopper, South exits the ♠6. West must cash his spades or South will be able to establish his ninth trick in clubs.

On the second last spade, East will have to abandon either hearts or diamonds. South will have to guess which suit East is no longer guarding. West has 5 known cards (5 spades) to East's 6 known cards (2 spades and 4 clubs). West is thus a favourite to have been dealt at least as many hearts and diamonds as East. West's most likely original shape is, therefore, 5440.

If East discards a diamond, so does South. On the last spade, a club is thrown from both hands. South can now succeed on a double squeeze (hearts being guarded by both defenders) regardless of what West returns.

On a heart return, for example, South wins the ♥A and unblocks the clubs. South returns to the closed hand in diamonds. The other diamond honour will squeeze East in hearts and clubs. A heart discard will leave West with the only defensive heart guard. South's remaining top club will then squeeze West in hearts and diamonds.
If, instead, East abandons hearts on the second last spade, South also pitches a heart. On the last spade a diamond is pitched from dummy and a club is thrown from the closed hand.

Again there will be a double squeeze, this time with diamonds guarded by both defenders. Assume that West switches to diamonds and South wins. South cashes the ♥A and the remaining club honour in the closed hand. A club to the ♣Q will squeeze West in hearts and diamonds. A diamond discard will leave East with the only defensive diamond guard. The ♥K will then squeeze East in diamonds and clubs.
